cards.gist: Creamy African cowpea marked with a single black spot
cards.guest: They're small, creamy Southern peas with a little black eye, slow-simmered until tender and earthy. It's the pea people eat on New Year's for luck.
cards.why: Not a true pea or a common bean but a cowpea, carried from West Africa to the South. A thin skin lets it cook tender in under an hour with no overnight soak, and it holds its shape with a creamy middle and an earthy, slightly nutty flavor.
cards.origin: West Africa, via the slave trade to the American South
cards.pairs: Collard greens, rice, cornbread, chow-chow, pepper vinegar
cards.notThis: Field peas is the family. Black-eyed is one member, beside crowders, lady peas and purple hulls.
cards.line: Braised black-eyed peas, smoked ham hock, chow-chow

cards.gist: Meat pounded thin, floured and pan-crisped like Southern chicken
cards.guest: It means the meat is pounded thin, floured and fried crisp just like fried chicken. Most often it's a beef steak, and it usually comes with a creamy pepper gravy.
cards.why: A tough, cheap cut, usually beef round run through a tenderizer, is pounded thin, dipped in egg or buttermilk and dredged in seasoned flour, then shallow-fried in hot fat. The ragged crust stays crisp under cream gravy, a floured cousin of the breadcrumbed schnitzel.
cards.origin: Texas and the Southern plains, likely from German schnitzel
cards.pairs: Cream gravy, mashed potatoes, green beans, biscuits
cards.line: Chicken-fried steak, pepper cream gravy, mashed potatoes
cards.prompt: A tough, cheap cut, usually beef round run through a tenderizer, is pounded thin, dipped in egg or buttermilk and dredged in seasoned flour, then shallow-__ in hot fat. The ragged crust stays crisp under cream gravy, a floured cousin of the breadcrumbed schnitzel.

cards.gist: Crunchy sweet-sour relish of cabbage, green tomato and pepper
cards.guest: It's a crunchy, tangy Southern relish of chopped cabbage, green tomatoes and peppers. A spoonful wakes up beans, greens or a rich plate of pork.
cards.why: End-of-garden vegetables, often the green tomatoes that will never ripen, are chopped, salted to draw out water, then cooked briefly in sweet vinegar with mustard seed and turmeric and jarred. The short cook keeps a crunch, and the acid cuts fat the way a pickle does.
cards.origin: Appalachian and Pennsylvania Dutch pantries, name of uncertain origin
cards.pairs: Field peas, pinto beans, collard greens, hot dogs, ham
cards.notThis: Not chutney, which is cooked down soft and fruit-led. This one stays crisp and vegetable-sharp.
cards.line: Smoked pork chop, black-eyed peas, house chow-chow

cards.gist: Shredded raw cabbage salad, dressed creamy or sharp with vinegar
cards.guest: It's crisp shredded cabbage in a tangy dressing, cool and crunchy. It's here to cut through the richness of barbecue and anything fried.
cards.why: Raw cabbage is shredded fine and dressed a while ahead, so salt and acid soften it slightly while it keeps its crunch. Creamy versions are mayonnaise-based; in the Carolinas it is often just vinegar, sugar and pepper, or reddened with ketchup.
cards.origin: Dutch koolsla, cabbage salad, brought to colonial New York
cards.pairs: Pulled pork, fried catfish, hushpuppies, sandwiches
cards.line: Pulled pork sandwich, vinegar coleslaw, pickles

cards.gist: Chopped cooked meat and potato, pan-crisped into a browned crust
cards.guest: Usually it's chopped meat and potatoes crisped in a hot pan, often with a runny egg on top. At Carolina barbecue joints it's a soft pork stew over rice.
cards.why: Born as a way to use leftovers: cooked meat, often corned or roast beef, is diced with potato and onion and pressed into a hot buttered pan, then left alone so the starch browns into a crust. In South Carolina barbecue joints, hash is instead a soft pork stew spooned over rice.
cards.note: The egg on top usually comes with a runny yolk. A guest can ask for it cooked through.
cards.origin: From the French hacher, to chop
cards.pairs: Fried or poached eggs, toast, hot sauce, and rice under Carolina hash
cards.line: Corned beef hash, two fried eggs, toast
cards.prompt: Born as a way to use leftovers: cooked meat, often corned or roast beef, is diced with potato and onion and pressed into a hot buttered pan, then left alone so the starch browns into a crust. In South Carolina barbecue joints, __ is instead a soft pork stew spooned over rice.

cards.gist: Thin cornmeal cake griddled in fat until the edges go lacy
cards.guest: They're thin cornmeal griddle cakes, crisp and lacy at the edges and soft in the middle. Think of a corn pancake with a toasty crunch.
cards.why: A loose cornmeal batter, once just meal, water and salt, now often with buttermilk, is poured into a hot greased skillet and flipped. Frying in fat crisps the thin edges. Some trace the name to hoe blades over a fire, others to an old word for a griddle.
cards.origin: Colonial Southern cornmeal bread, kin to the New England johnnycake
cards.pairs: Butter, sorghum, country ham, greens and pot likker
cards.notThis: Not skillet cornbread, which is poured thick into a pan and baked. These are thin and flipped on a griddle.
cards.line: Buttermilk hoecakes, sorghum butter, country ham

cards.gist: Whole corn kernels steeped in alkali until puffed and chewy
cards.guest: It's corn that's been soaked and cooked until the kernels puff up big and soft, a little chewy. It tastes like a warm corn tortilla.
cards.why: Dried field corn is cooked in an alkali, slaked lime or lye, which loosens the hull so it slips off and swells the starch. The same process makes masa for tortillas, so hominy shares that toasty flavor. It eats plump and chewy, and ground coarse it becomes hominy grits.
cards.origin: From a Powhatan word, the same corn as Mexican pozole
cards.pairs: Braised pork, chiles, greens, butter and black pepper
cards.notThis: Not grits, though grits can be ground from it. Hominy is whole, puffy kernels you can count.
cards.line: Braised pork shoulder, stewed hominy, charred onion

cards.gist: Lowcountry rice steamed in the broth of cowpeas and smoked pork
cards.guest: It's a Southern rice and peas dish, slow-cooked with smoky pork and onion. It's the traditional New Year's Day luck dish, with greens and cornbread.
cards.why: Field peas, usually black-eyed, are simmered with smoked pork, then rice is cooked in that seasoned liquid so each grain takes up the smoke and pea flavor. It comes from the Gullah Geechee rice kitchens of coastal Carolina, kin to West African and Caribbean rice and peas.
cards.origin: Lowcountry South Carolina, from Gullah Geechee cooks
cards.pairs: Collard greens, cornbread, pepper vinegar, hot sauce
cards.line: Hoppin' John, braised collards, skillet cornbread

cards.gist: Native Southern grape, thick-skinned, musky and often dark purple
cards.guest: It's the South's own native grape, big and thick-skinned with a sweet, musky, floral taste. You'll see it in wine, jelly and pie.
cards.why: A separate species from European wine grapes, native to the humid Southeast. The berries are big, often an inch or more across, in loose clusters, with a tough skin and a few seeds around slippery pulp. The flavor is musky and floral, closer to a Concord than a table grape.
cards.note: Most people pop the pulp out of the tough skin, then spit out or swallow the seeds.
cards.origin: Native to the Southeastern United States, ripe late summer into fall
cards.line: Grilled quail, muscadine jus, Carolina Gold rice

cards.gist: Bronze-green type of the Southeast's native thick-skinned grape
cards.guest: It's a golden-bronze muscadine, the old native grape of the Carolinas. Thick skin, juicy center and a honeyed, floral sweetness.
cards.why: The first named variety of the muscadine grape, found growing wild on North Carolina's coast and now its state fruit. The skin ripens greenish bronze instead of purple, and it eats a touch sweeter and more floral than the dark kind, with the same thick hull and seeds.
cards.origin: Named for the Scuppernong River in northeastern North Carolina
cards.notThis: Not a separate species. Every scuppernong is a muscadine, but most muscadines are dark, not bronze.
cards.line: Scuppernong sorbet, mint

cards.gist: Amber syrup boiled down from the pressed juice of a tall cane grass
cards.guest: Sorghum is a syrup made by boiling down the juice of a sugary cane grass. Think molasses, but lighter, earthier and a little tangy.
cards.why: Stalks of sweet sorghum, a grass first grown in Africa, are crushed each fall and the green juice is boiled in open pans until thick. It is thinner and milder than molasses, with an earthy, grassy, slightly sour edge that cuts rich food.
cards.origin: African grass; the syrup is a fall tradition in Kentucky and Tennessee
cards.pairs: Hot biscuits and butter, glazed pork, pecan pie
cards.notThis: Not true molasses, which is left over from making sugar. Older Southerners still call it sorghum molasses.
cards.line: Sorghum-glazed pork belly, braised collards
cards.prompt: Stalks of sweet __, a grass first grown in Africa, are crushed each fall and the green juice is boiled in open pans until thick. It is thinner and milder than molasses, with an earthy, grassy, slightly sour edge that cuts rich food.

cards.gist: Thin pan sauce of country ham drippings lifted with black coffee
cards.guest: It's a thin, salty sauce from pan-fried country ham, made with black coffee. Spoon it over the ham, grits or a split biscuit.
cards.why: Slices of country ham fry until their fat and browned bits coat the skillet. Black coffee, sometimes with water, goes in to lift them. It is left unthickened, so it stays thin and brothy: salty, smoky and a little bitter, more jus than gravy.
cards.origin: American South; said to be named for the reddish eye of fat in the bowl
cards.pairs: Country ham, stone-ground grits, biscuits
cards.line: Country ham, red-eye gravy, stone-ground grits
cards.prompt: Slices of country ham fry until their fat and browned bits coat the skillet. Black coffee, sometimes with water, goes in to lift them. It is left unthickened, so it stays thin and brothy: salty, smoky and a little bitter, more jus than __.

cards.gist: Warm summer mix of sweet corn kernels and butter beans
cards.guest: It's sweet summer corn and butter beans cooked together, often with tomato or okra. Sweet, creamy and bright, it tastes like peak summer.
cards.why: A Native American dish of corn and beans, adopted across the South with lima or butter beans. Fresh corn brings sugar and pop, the beans a creamy, starchy bite, and butter or bacon fat ties them together. Think of it as a warm corn and bean salad.
cards.origin: From Narragansett msickquatash, meaning boiled corn kernels
cards.pairs: Fried chicken, grilled fish, pork chops
cards.line: Seared scallops, summer succotash, brown butter

cards.gist: Broad, sturdy cabbage-family leaves braised long with smoked pork
cards.guest: They're big, sturdy Southern greens, simmered low with smoky pork until silky. Earthier than spinach, milder than kale, with a little vinegar bite.
cards.why: The same species as cabbage and kale, grown as flat paddle leaves that never form a head. Their tough cell walls need a long braise, usually with smoked pork, to turn silky. A frost sweetens them, and the cooking broth is saved as pot likker.
cards.origin: From colewort, an old English word for cabbage plants
cards.pairs: Cornbread, pepper vinegar, black-eyed peas
cards.line: Smoked pork chop, braised collard greens, cornbread

cards.gist: Smoky, savory broth left behind by long-simmered greens
cards.guest: It's the broth the greens cook in, slow-simmered with smoked pork. Smoky and savory, it's made for dunking cornbread.
cards.why: Greens simmer for an hour or more with smoked ham hock or turkey, onion and water. The pork's smoke and fat and the greens' minerals end up in the liquid, so it tastes like a light, smoky ham broth with a green, slightly bitter edge.
cards.origin: Southern spelling of pot liquor, the liquid left in the pot
cards.pairs: Cornbread for dunking, collards, field peas
cards.line: Braised greens in pot likker, skillet cornbread

cards.gist: Umbrella name for Southern summer cowpea kinds: crowder, lady, zipper
cards.guest: Field peas are Southern summer beans, shelled fresh and simmered low with a little smoked pork. They turn creamy and earthy in their own savory broth.
cards.why: They are cowpeas, one species carried from West Africa, not the green garden pea. Shelled fresh in summer or dried, and simmered with smoked pork, they cook creamy and nutty and make their own broth. Crowder, lady, zipper and purple hull are common kinds.
cards.origin: West African cowpeas, named for the farm fields they grew in
cards.pairs: Cornbread, sliced tomatoes, pepper vinegar, rice
cards.notThis: Not green garden peas, and not only black-eyed peas: those are one kind among crowders, lady peas and zippers.
cards.line: Summer field peas, sliced tomato, pepper vinegar
cards.prompt: They are cowpeas, one species carried from West Africa, not the green garden __. Shelled fresh in summer or dried, and simmered with smoked pork, they cook creamy and nutty and make their own broth. Crowder, lady, zipper and purple hull are common kinds.

cards.gist: Old Lowcountry name for sesame seed, toasted for nutty crunch
cards.guest: Benne is the old Southern word for sesame. Toasted, it brings a nutty crunch, and in Charleston it goes into thin, crisp benne wafers.
cards.why: Enslaved West Africans brought the seed and its name to the Carolina Lowcountry. Heirloom benne holds less oil than modern sesame, so it toasts deeper and tastes earthier, almost bitter. Menus often use the word for any sesame.
cards.origin: From a West African word for sesame, carried to the Carolina coast
cards.line: Benne-crusted flounder, collard greens, brown butter
cards.prompt: Enslaved West Africans brought the seed and its name to the Carolina Lowcountry. Heirloom __ holds less oil than modern sesame, so it toasts deeper and tastes earthier, almost bitter. Menus often use the word for any sesame.

cards.gist: Heirloom Lowcountry long grain, nearly lost and then revived
cards.guest: It's the heirloom rice the Carolina coast was built on, nearly lost and brought back. It cooks up fluffy but a little creamy, with a clean, sweet flavor.
cards.why: Grown in South Carolina by the late 1600s, it made planters rich on the skill of enslaved West African rice growers, then nearly vanished after 1900. It can cook up separate like long grain or turn creamy when stirred, closer to risotto rice.
cards.origin: South Carolina Lowcountry, named for its golden hull in the field
cards.line: Carolina Gold rice pilau, shrimp, smoked sausage
cards.prompt: Grown in South __ by the late 1600s, it made planters rich on the skill of enslaved West African __ growers, then nearly vanished after 1900. It can cook up separate like long grain or turn creamy when stirred, closer to risotto __.

cards.gist: Sharp cheddar bound with mayonnaise and sweet red peppers
cards.guest: It's the South's favorite spread, sharp cheddar and sweet red peppers mashed with mayo. Rich, tangy and a little sweet, great on a cracker or a burger.
cards.why: Grated cheddar is folded into mayonnaise with diced pimentos, small sweet red peppers sold roasted in jars. The mayo makes it creamy and spreadable, the cheddar brings tang. It began around 1900 as a Northern factory product and became a Southern staple.
cards.pairs: Saltine crackers, celery, fried green tomatoes, burgers
cards.line: Pimento cheese, pepper jelly, benne crackers
cards.prompt: Grated cheddar is folded into mayonnaise with diced __, small sweet red peppers sold roasted in jars. The mayo makes it creamy and spreadable, the cheddar brings tang. It began around 1900 as a Northern factory product and became a Southern staple.

cards.gist: Crusty skillet-baked quick bread of cornmeal and buttermilk
cards.guest: It's a cornmeal bread baked in a hot iron skillet, so the edges come out crisp and golden. Tender inside with a real toasted corn flavor, and best with butter.
cards.why: Cornmeal, buttermilk and egg are leavened with baking soda and poured into a skillet already hot with fat, which fries the crust as it bakes. Southern versions are less sweet and more corn-forward. Northern ones are sweeter and cakier.
cards.notThis: Not hoecakes, thin cornmeal cakes cooked on a griddle. Cornbread is poured into a pan and baked.
cards.line: Skillet cornbread, sorghum butter

cards.gist: Deep-fried balls of cornmeal batter, served beside fried fish
cards.guest: They're little fritters of seasoned cornmeal batter, fried golden. Crunchy outside, soft and a bit oniony inside, and the classic side for fried fish.
cards.why: A thick batter of cornmeal, buttermilk, egg and onion is dropped by the spoonful into hot oil, where it puffs into a crisp shell around a steamy, cakey middle. Think cornbread batter, fried. The tale of cooks tossing them to quiet dogs is folklore.
cards.note: Often fried in the same oil as the fish and shrimp. Ask the kitchen when a guest needs to know.
cards.pairs: Fried catfish, fried shrimp, coleslaw, tartar sauce
cards.line: Fried catfish, hushpuppies, slaw, comeback sauce

cards.gist: Ridged green seed pod, silky when stewed and crisp when fried
cards.guest: It's a green seed pod, a cousin of hibiscus. Fried, it's crisp and nutty, and simmered in a stew it turns silky and thickens the pot.
cards.why: The pods hold a slippery sap, mucilage, released when they are cut and cooked in liquid. That is what thickens gumbo, a word from a Bantu name for okra. Frying and high heat keep it crisp. Acid, like tomato or vinegar, cuts the slick.
cards.origin: African plant, carried to the South through the slave trade
cards.line: Cornmeal-fried okra, comeback sauce
cards.prompt: The pods hold a slippery sap, mucilage, released when they are cut and cooked in liquid. That is what thickens gumbo, a word from a Bantu name for __. Frying and high heat keep it crisp. Acid, like tomato or vinegar, cuts the slick.

cards.gist: Raw groundnuts simmered in brine, shell on, until soft
cards.guest: They're a roadside Southern classic, peanuts simmered in the shell in salty water until soft like a bean. Crack one open and slurp the brine.
cards.why: Best made with green peanuts, freshly dug and not dried. Hours of boiling in heavy brine soften the nut to a tender, buttery texture and salt it through the shell. They taste closer to a tender cooked bean than a roasted nut.
cards.note: Served in the shell. Guests crack them open and set the shells aside, so bring a bowl.
cards.origin: Southern roadside snack, the official state snack of South Carolina
cards.line: Warm Cajun boiled peanuts, cold beer
cards.prompt: Best made with green __, freshly dug and not dried. Hours of boiling in heavy brine soften the nut to a tender, buttery texture and salt it through the shell. They taste closer to a tender cooked bean than a roasted nut.

cards.gist: Bottle of whole hot chilies steeped in sharp acid, for greens
cards.guest: It's a bottle of little hot peppers soaking in vinegar. A few shakes brighten greens or peas with a sharp, spicy tang, and it sits on most Southern tables.
cards.why: Small hot peppers, often tabasco or bird chilies, are packed into a bottle and covered with white vinegar. Over days the vinegar takes on their heat while staying thin and clear, and the bottle is topped up as it empties. Its acid cuts pork-rich greens.
cards.notThis: Not a blended hot sauce. It stays thin and clear, and the whole peppers stay in the bottle.
cards.line: Braised collards, pot likker, pepper vinegar

cards.gist: Cooked fully submerged in water at a full, rolling bubble
cards.guest: It's cooked right in boiling water, which keeps the flavor clean and sweet, so the lobster or potatoes really shine.
cards.why: A rolling boil is as hot as water gets at sea level, 100 C (212 F), and the bubbles keep everything moving. That suits pasta, potatoes, lobster and crab, which want fast, even heat. Delicate fish and meat toughen at a hard boil, so kitchens simmer or poach those.
cards.pairs: Lobster with drawn butter, potatoes with parsley, corned beef with mustard
cards.notThis: Not simmered: a simmer is a lazy bubble, gentler on meat. Boiled means a full, rolling boil.
cards.line: Boiled Maine lobster, drawn butter, corn, new potatoes

cards.gist: Often browned, then cooked slowly, covered, in a little liquid
cards.guest: It's usually seared first, then cooked slowly in a covered pot with wine or stock for hours. It comes out fork-tender, with the cooking liquid as its sauce.
cards.why: Braising suits tough, hard-working cuts like short rib, shank and cheek. The meat sits partly in liquid under a lid at gentle heat for hours, and its connective tissue melts into gelatin. That makes the meat silky and turns the liquid into a glossy sauce.
cards.notThis: Not stewed: a stew cuts meat small and covers it in liquid. A braise keeps big pieces, half submerged.
cards.line: Red wine braised short rib, creamy polenta, gremolata

cards.gist: Soaked in salted water before cooking to season and stay juicy
cards.guest: It's soaked in salt water before it's cooked, so it stays juicy and seasoned all the way through. Pork chops and turkey love it.
cards.why: Over hours, salt water works into the meat and loosens its proteins, so they hold on to more of their own juice in the heat. The result is juicier, evenly seasoned meat, which is why lean pork, chicken and turkey are brined most. Sugar and herbs often ride along.
cards.notThis: Not pickled: a quick pickle sits in vinegar and turns sour. A meat brine only seasons, then the meat is cooked.
cards.line: Brined pork chop, apple mostarda, braised greens
cards.prompt: Over hours, salt water works into the meat and loosens its proteins, so they hold on to more of their own juice in the heat. The result is juicier, evenly seasoned meat, which is why lean pork, chicken and turkey are __ most. Sugar and herbs often ride along.

cards.gist: Cooked until sugar, natural or added, browns to a nutty sweetness
cards.guest: It's cooked until its sugars turn golden brown and sweet, the way onions cook down jammy and rich.
cards.why: Heat breaks sugar down into hundreds of new compounds that taste nutty, toasty and a little bitter, like the top of a crème brûlée. Strictly that is sugar alone; browning meat is a separate reaction that needs protein. Menus use it loosely for any slow, deep browning of onions or fruit.
cards.notThis: Not seared: a sear browns meat protein in minutes. Caramelizing browns sugars, usually slowly.
cards.line: Burger, caramelized onions, gruyère, brioche bun

cards.gist: Cooked slowly and fully submerged in fat at low heat
cards.guest: It's usually duck leg, cooked slowly in its own fat until it's meltingly tender. Then it's crisped up so the skin crackles.
cards.why: The meat is salted overnight, covered in fat and cooked gently for hours, well below frying heat, so it poaches rather than fries. It turns silky and pulls from the bone. Before refrigeration the fat seal kept it for months. Garlic or tomato confit is cooked the same way in oil.
cards.origin: French, from confire, to preserve
cards.notThis: Not fried: confit fat stays far below frying heat, so the meat poaches soft. Fried food browns fast.
cards.line: Duck leg confit, white beans, frisée, mustard
cards.prompt: The meat is salted overnight, covered in fat and cooked gently for hours, well below frying heat, so it poaches rather than fries. It turns silky and pulls from the bone. Before refrigeration the fat seal kept it for months. Garlic or tomato __ is cooked the same way in oil.

cards.gist: Salted, then often dried or smoked, to firm it and make it keep
cards.guest: It's been salted, and sometimes smoked or aged, the way prosciutto or lox is. That firms it up and gives it a deep, savory flavor.
cards.why: Salt pulls water out of meat or fish, and with less water left, spoiling microbes struggle. The flesh firms, turns translucent and concentrates in flavor. Many cures add sugar, and most ham and bacon get nitrite, which keeps them pink. Bacon is cooked before eating.
cards.note: Prosciutto crudo, bresaola, gravlax and lox are cured, not cooked, and are usually served raw.
cards.notThis: Not smoked: smoke adds flavor, salt does the curing. Plenty of cured meat never sees smoke.
cards.line: House-cured salmon, crème fraîche, rye, pickled shallot
cards.prompt: Salt pulls water out of meat or fish, and with less water left, spoiling microbes struggle. The flesh firms, turns translucent and concentrates in flavor. Many __ add sugar, and most ham and bacon get nitrite, which keeps them pink. Bacon is cooked before eating.

cards.gist: Cooked in hot oil until the outside turns crisp and golden
cards.guest: It's cooked in hot oil, so the outside turns crisp and golden while the inside stays moist. Often it's battered or breaded first.
cards.why: Frying oil runs near 175 to 190 C (350 to 375 F), far hotter than boiling water, so the surface dries and browns into a crust while steam keeps the center moist. Deep frying submerges the food; pan frying uses oil partway up. Batter or breading gives the crunch.
cards.note: Many kitchens share one fryer across dishes, so ask what else is cooked in the same oil.
cards.notThis: Not sautéed: a sauté uses a slick of fat and constant tossing. Fried food sits in enough oil to crisp.
cards.line: Buttermilk fried chicken, hot honey, pickles

cards.gist: Cooked on a grate right over an open flame or glowing coals
cards.guest: It's cooked over an open flame, which gives it those dark grill marks and a smoky, charred edge.
cards.why: Heat radiates up from flame or coals, and the hot bars sear stripes where they touch. Fat and juices drip onto the fire and rise back as flavorful smoke. It is fast, high heat, so it suits steaks, fish, vegetables and anything thin enough to cook through before it burns.
cards.note: A grilled cheese or grilled sandwich is cooked on a flat griddle, not over a flame.
cards.notThis: Not smoked, which is slow, low heat in wood smoke, and not blackened, a spice crust seared in a skillet.
cards.line: Grilled swordfish, salsa verde, charred lemon

cards.gist: Kept in a sour liquid, usually vinegar, so it turns tangy and sharp
cards.guest: It's been soaked in tangy vinegar, so it comes out bright, sour and often a little crunchy. It's there to cut through the richer things on the plate.
cards.why: Vegetables, fruit, eggs or fish sit in vinegar with salt and often sugar and spices. The acid seasons them all the way through, and raw vegetables keep their crunch. Quick pickles are ready in hours; fermented pickles get their sourness from bacteria over days.
cards.notThis: Not brined: brining soaks meat in salt water before cooking, while a pickle is sour and eaten as it is.
cards.line: Pork belly, pickled mustard seeds, charred scallion
cards.prompt: Vegetables, fruit, eggs or fish sit in vinegar with salt and often sugar and spices. The acid seasons them all the way through, and raw vegetables keep their crunch. Quick __ are ready in hours; fermented __ get their sourness from bacteria over days.

cards.gist: Cooked in hot liquid that never bubbles, so it stays soft and moist
cards.guest: It's cooked gently in a flavorful liquid that never quite bubbles, so it stays tender and juicy. It's one of the gentlest ways to cook fish, eggs or chicken.
cards.why: The liquid, water, stock, wine, milk, butter or oil, stays below a simmer, about 71 to 82 C (160 to 180 F). Proteins firm slowly without squeezing out much juice, so fish flakes silkily and eggs set around a soft yolk. Nothing browns, so the flavor stays clean.
cards.note: A poached egg normally arrives with a runny, not fully set, yolk.
cards.notThis: Not boiled: boiling bubbles hard and toughens delicate food, while poaching keeps the liquid barely trembling.
cards.line: Poached halibut, fennel, saffron broth

cards.gist: Made to keep for months by any of several methods, not just one
cards.guest: It's been made to last, with salt, sugar or vinegar, the way cooks kept summer food for winter. That also concentrates the flavor, so a little goes a long way.
cards.why: It is an umbrella word, not one technique. Salt, sugar and drying pull water out of food, acid slows spoilage, and time does the rest. Texture softens and taste deepens: preserved lemon rind turns silky and salty, preserved cherries turn syrupy.
cards.notThis: Not fresh: the item was made weeks or months ahead, and it tastes saltier, sweeter or sourer than the raw ingredient.
cards.line: Roast chicken, preserved lemon, green olives
cards.prompt: It is an umbrella word, not one technique. Salt, sugar and drying pull water out of food, acid slows spoilage, and time does the rest. Texture softens and taste deepens: __ lemon rind turns silky and salty, __ cherries turn syrupy.

cards.gist: Blended thick and completely smooth, firm enough to hold its shape
cards.guest: It's been blended until it's completely smooth, like a velvety spread on the plate. You get the flavor of the vegetable or fruit in a rich, silky form.
cards.why: Food, usually cooked soft first, is blended or pushed through a fine sieve until no fiber or lump is left, so it eats silky and dense. Kitchens often loosen it with butter, cream or stock, which is why a purée can taste richer than the vegetable. A mash keeps some texture.
cards.origin: French purer, to strain or make pure
cards.notThis: Not a coulis: a coulis is a thin sauce you pour, while a purée is thick enough to hold its shape on the plate.
cards.line: Seared scallops, cauliflower purée, brown butter
cards.prompt: Food, usually cooked soft first, is blended or pushed through a fine sieve until no fiber or lump is left, so it eats silky and dense. Kitchens often loosen it with butter, cream or stock, which is why a __ can taste richer than the vegetable. A mash keeps some texture.

cards.gist: Cooked by dry heat in an oven until browned outside and tender inside
cards.guest: It's cooked in a hot oven, so the outside browns and caramelizes while the inside stays juicy. That browning is where the deep, savory flavor comes from.
cards.why: Hot, dry air surrounds the food on every side. The surface dries and browns, building a savory crust on meat and sweet, caramelized edges on vegetables, while the center cooks more gently. Unlike braising, no liquid goes in, and big cuts rest before carving.
cards.note: Roast beef and lamb are usually carved pink, at medium rare, unless asked otherwise.
cards.notThis: Not pan-roasted: that starts in a skillet for the crust and finishes in the oven, usually for a single portion.
cards.line: Roasted chicken, root vegetables, pan jus

cards.gist: Cooked fast in a little fat in a hot pan, tossed to cook evenly
cards.guest: It's cooked quickly in a hot pan with a little butter or oil, so it stays fresh and bright with lightly golden edges. The quick heat keeps it light.
cards.why: Small or thin pieces go into a hot, shallow pan with just enough fat to coat it and are tossed or stirred. High heat and little fat brown the edges before the inside overcooks, so greens stay vivid and mushrooms turn golden.
cards.origin: French sauter, to jump, from tossing food in the pan
cards.notThis: Not fried: frying uses a deeper layer of oil, while a sauté uses only a thin film of fat and keeps the food moving.
cards.line: Sautéed spinach, garlic, lemon

cards.gist: Browned hard on a very hot surface to give it a dark, flavorful crust
cards.guest: It's cooked in a very hot pan just long enough to build a deep golden crust, so you get a caramelized outside with a tender, juicy inside.
cards.why: Dry food meets metal hot enough for the Maillard reaction, the browning of proteins and sugars that makes crust and roasted flavor. It takes a minute or two, so tuna or scallops can stay rare inside. It builds flavor; it does not seal in juice.
cards.note: Seared tuna is usually served rare, and seared scallops translucent in the center.
cards.notThis: Not blackened: blackening coats the food in spices and chars that coating, while searing browns the food itself.
cards.line: Seared scallops, sweet corn, brown butter

cards.gist: Cooked gently in liquid with small bubbles breaking now and then
cards.guest: It's cooked slowly in a gently bubbling liquid, so the flavors have time to meld and the meat or beans turn tender. Think of a good soup or a pot of beans.
cards.why: The liquid sits just under boiling, about 85 to 96 C (185 to 205 F), with small bubbles breaking now and then. That is hot enough to soften tough cuts, beans and grains and pull flavor into a stock, yet calm enough not to shred meat or cloud a broth.
cards.notThis: Not poached, which is cooler with no bubbles, or boiled, which rolls hard and can toughen meat and break up delicate food.
cards.line: Simmered white beans, rosemary, olive oil

cards.gist: Flavored, and often slowly cooked, by the fumes of smoldering wood
cards.guest: It's been cooked or just flavored in the smoke of smoldering wood, so it picks up a deep, sweet smokiness, like good barbecue or smoked salmon.
cards.why: Smoldering hardwood gives off compounds that settle on the food and color it. Hot smoking also cooks it low and slow, which is how brisket goes tender. Cold smoking only flavors, so cold-smoked salmon stays silky and uncooked. Fruit woods are mild; hickory is bold.
cards.note: A pink ring just under the crust of smoked meat is normal. The smoke gases make it.
cards.notThis: Not the same as cured. Salt cures, smoke flavors, and many hams and bacons get both.
cards.line: Smoked half chicken, white barbecue sauce, pickles
cards.prompt: Smoldering hardwood gives off compounds that settle on the food and color it. Hot smoking also cooks it low and slow, which is how brisket goes tender. Cold smoking only flavors, so cold-__ salmon stays silky and uncooked. Fruit woods are mild; hickory is bold.

cards.gist: Sealed in a bag and held in a warm water bath at its exact doneness
cards.guest: It's cooked slowly in a warm water bath set to exactly the doneness we want, and meats get a sear at the end. It comes out tender and evenly cooked.
cards.why: The food is vacuum sealed and set in water held at the target temperature itself, well below a simmer, so it can never overshoot. A steak comes out pink from edge to edge with no gray band. It gets no crust in the bag, so kitchens sear it afterward.
cards.note: Steak, chops and duck come out evenly pink by design. Take any doneness request to the kitchen.
cards.origin: French for under vacuum, a restaurant method since the 1970s
cards.notThis: Not poached. A poach sits in open, barely bubbling liquid; this sits sealed in a bath held at its exact doneness.
cards.line: Sous vide pork chop, charred peach, mustard jus

cards.gist: Greens heated just until they slump, still bright and barely cooked
cards.guest: The greens are warmed just until they soften, so they are tender but still fresh and bright. Think of a warm salad.
cards.why: A short hit of heat from a hot pan, hot broth or a warm dressing bursts the leaf's cell membranes, so it goes limp and releases water. Stopped there, the greens stay vivid and fresh tasting. Spinach, chard and tender lettuces take seconds; cooked longer, they turn dull and stewed.
cards.origin: Southern and Appalachian cooks call hot bacon dressing on lettuce killed lettuce
cards.notThis: Close to a quick sauté, but stopped the moment the leaves soften, before anything browns.
cards.line: Wilted spinach, garlic, lemon, chili flake

cards.gist: Dipped briefly in boiling water, then usually chilled in ice water
cards.guest: It gets a quick dip in boiling water and then an ice bath, so the vegetables stay bright green with a little snap.
cards.why: A minute or two in heavily salted boiling water softens the outside, sets green color and loosens skins; the ice bath stops the cooking right there. Kitchens blanch ahead so a vegetable only needs a quick finish on the line. Blanched almonds are simply almonds with the skins slipped off.
cards.origin: From French blanchir, to whiten
cards.notThis: Not boiled. Boiling cooks food through in the water; blanching is a quick dip that stops short.
cards.line: Blanched haricots verts, brown butter, almonds
cards.prompt: A minute or two in heavily salted boiling water softens the outside, sets green color and loosens skins; the ice bath stops the cooking right there. Kitchens blanch ahead so a vegetable only needs a quick finish on the line. __ almonds are simply almonds with the skins slipped off.

cards.gist: Cooked by hot vapor rising from water below, without touching it
cards.guest: It's cooked gently over boiling water, so it stays moist and tender and keeps its clean, natural flavor.
cards.why: The food sits in a basket or on a rack above the water, and steam carries heat in fast without the surface ever drying or browning. Nothing leaches into a pot of water, so fish stays delicate and vegetables keep their color. Dumplings and bao get their soft, pillowy skins this way.
cards.note: Steamed fish is often served whole, on the bone, so mention the bones to the guest.
cards.pairs: Ginger and scallion, soy sauce, sesame oil, jasmine rice
cards.notThis: Not poached. Poached food sits in the liquid; steamed food sits above it, out of the water.
cards.line: Steamed black bass, ginger, scallion, soy

cards.gist: Changed slowly by live microbes, turning tangy, funky or savory
cards.guest: It's been slowly transformed by yeasts and bacteria, like sourdough or kimchi, so it has a tangy, deep, savory flavor you only get with time.
cards.why: Yeasts, bacteria and molds turn sugars into acid, alcohol or gas, and enzymes break proteins into savory depth. That makes the tang in kimchi and yogurt, the funk in miso and fish sauce, and the rise in sourdough. Time does the work: days for kraut, months or years for miso.
cards.origin: From Latin fervere, to boil, for the bubbling of a live ferment
cards.notThis: Not pickled. A quick pickle gets its sour from added vinegar; a ferment makes its own sour.
cards.line: Fermented chili glaze, crispy pork belly, herbs

cards.gist: Fat melted slowly out of meat or skin, leaving the rest crisp
cards.guest: The fat is slowly melted out so the skin crisps instead of going rubbery, and that fat is often saved to cook with, like duck fat for potatoes.
cards.why: Gentle heat melts the fat inside skin or fatty meat so it runs out into the pan. Take it slowly and the skin thins and crisps; rush it and the outside burns over a layer of soft fat. The fat left behind is saved and used: lard, duck fat, schmaltz, tallow.
cards.note: Duck breast with rendered skin is classically served pink, at medium rare.
cards.notThis: Not confit. Confit cooks meat submerged in fat; rendering pulls the fat out of the meat.
cards.line: Duck breast, skin rendered crisp, cherry jus

cards.gist: Dipped in butter, crusted in spice and cooked dark in a hot skillet
cards.guest: It's coated in a Cajun spice blend and seared in a very hot cast iron pan, so it gets a dark, spicy crust while the inside stays tender and juicy.
cards.why: The fillet is dipped in melted butter, packed with paprika, cayenne, thyme and garlic, and dropped in a skillet heated until it smokes. The butter solids and spices toast almost black in a minute or two, while the inside stays moist. The dark color is toasted spice, not burnt fish.
cards.note: Blackened tuna is usually served rare in the center, and steak is cooked to order.
cards.origin: New Orleans, made famous by chef Paul Prudhomme in the early 1980s
cards.notThis: Not simply seared. A sear browns plain meat; this builds a dark crust of spice and butter.
cards.line: Blackened redfish, dirty rice, lemon butter

cards.gist: Browned hard on the stove, then finished in a hot oven in one skillet
cards.guest: It's seared in a hot skillet for a crisp, golden crust, then slid into the oven to finish, so the inside stays juicy and cooks evenly.
cards.why: Hard browning on the stove builds the crust, then the same ovenproof skillet goes into a hot oven. Surrounding heat cooks thick cuts through evenly without burning the outside, and many kitchens finish with a butter baste. Searing alone suits thinner pieces.
cards.notThis: Seared is stove only and roasted is oven only. Pan-roasting does both in one skillet, which suits thick chops, breasts and fillets.
cards.line: Pan-roasted halibut, brown butter, capers, lemon

cards.gist: Coarse, heavily smoked Louisiana pork sausage with garlic and cayenne
cards.guest: It's Louisiana's smoked pork sausage, coarse and garlicky with a peppery kick. It's what gives gumbo and jambalaya their deep, smoky backbone.
cards.why: Chunks of pork shoulder, not a fine grind, are seasoned with garlic, black pepper and cayenne, cased and smoked hard, often over pecan wood. It comes out firm, dark and smoky enough to season a whole pot. Think kielbasa, but coarser and hotter.
cards.pairs: Gumbo, jambalaya, red beans and rice, shrimp and grits
cards.notThis: Not tasso, its smokehouse partner, a solid spiced slab of shoulder. French andouille, its ancestor, is a tripe sausage.
cards.line: Chicken and andouille gumbo, Carolina Gold rice

cards.gist: Paprika-red pork sausage, dry-cured in Spain and sold raw in Mexico
cards.guest: It's a garlicky pork sausage stained deep red. Sliced like salami it's the cured Spanish kind, and crumbled it's the fresh Mexican kind, which is spicier.
cards.why: Two products share one word. Spanish chorizo is chopped pork cured with pimentón, the smoked paprika that gives it color and smoke, then dried until sliceable. Mexican chorizo is raw ground pork with dried chiles and vinegar, cooked loose so its red fat stains the dish.
cards.note: Ask the kitchen which kind. Cured Spanish chorizo is air-dried, not cooked, and sliced as is. Fresh Mexican chorizo is always cooked.
cards.origin: Spain and Portugal, remade in Mexico with local chiles
cards.line: Steamed clams, Spanish chorizo, white wine, grilled bread
cards.prompt: Two products share one word. Spanish __ is chopped pork cured with pimentón, the smoked paprika that gives it color and smoke, then dried until sliceable. Mexican __ is raw ground pork with dried chiles and vinegar, cooked loose so its red fat stains the dish.

cards.gist: Italian dry-cured pork neck muscle, marbled and sliced paper thin
cards.guest: It's dry-cured pork neck, sliced thin like prosciutto but with more marbling and a little more spice. Rich, tender and slightly sweet.
cards.why: The muscle running from the neck into the shoulder is salted, rubbed with pepper and spices, cased and hung to dry for months. Several small muscles meet here, so ribbons of fat run through the lean, making it richer and more seasoned than prosciutto and softer than salami.
cards.note: A dry-cured coppa is air-dried, not cooked, and is served as is in thin slices.
cards.notThis: Not prosciutto, which is the whole hind leg cured with salt alone. Coppa is a smaller, spiced, fattier muscle.
cards.line: Coppa, pickled peppers, grilled sourdough

cards.gist: American pork leg, dry-salted, often smoked, then aged for months
cards.guest: It's the South's answer to prosciutto, a pork leg packed in salt and aged for months. It's salty, deep and a little funky, so a thin slice goes a long way.
cards.why: A whole pork leg is packed in dry salt, often with sugar, usually smoked over hickory, then hung through a summer or longer. It loses water and concentrates, so it eats firm, intensely salty and savory. City ham is brined instead, so it stays moist and mild.
cards.note: Served two ways: shaved uncooked like prosciutto, or sliced thicker and pan-fried. Ask the kitchen which.
cards.pairs: Biscuits, red-eye gravy, grits, melon, pickles
cards.line: Shaved country ham, buttermilk biscuits, sorghum butter
cards.prompt: A whole pork leg is packed in dry salt, often with sugar, usually smoked over hickory, then hung through a summer or longer. It loses water and concentrates, so it eats firm, intensely salty and savory. City __ is brined instead, so it stays moist and mild.

cards.gist: Italian cured pork jowl, unsmoked, richer and fattier than belly
cards.guest: It's cured pork jowl, the fatty cheek, like an unsmoked Italian bacon with richer, silkier fat. It's the classic pork in carbonara and amatriciana.
cards.why: The jowl is rubbed with salt, black pepper and sometimes herbs, then hung to dry for weeks. It is mostly fat with streaks of lean, and that fat is firmer and more flavorful than belly fat. In a pan it renders into crisp pieces and a savory fat that becomes the sauce.
cards.note: Nearly always cooked: diced and rendered until crisp, not sliced for a board.
cards.notThis: Not pancetta, which is cured belly, leaner and milder, and not bacon, which is smoked belly. This is the jowl.
cards.line: Bucatini all'amatriciana, guanciale, pecorino

cards.gist: Italian cured pork back fat, aged with salt and herbs, shaved thin
cards.guest: It's pure pork back fat cured with salt, rosemary and garlic until it's silky and sweet. Shaved thin over warm toast, it melts like butter.
cards.why: Thick slabs of fat from the pig's back are layered with sea salt, rosemary, garlic and spices and cured for months, traditionally in marble tubs in Colonnata, Tuscany. The cure firms and perfumes it, so a thin slice turns translucent and melts on anything warm.
cards.note: Served uncooked in paper-thin slices, best laid on something warm so it softens.
cards.notThis: Not lard, the rendered cooking fat. Lardo is a cured solid slab, sliced and eaten like other cured meats.
cards.line: Grilled sourdough, lardo, rosemary, sea salt

cards.gist: Spanish air-dried whole pork loin, lean, rubbed with smoked paprika
cards.guest: It's Spanish cured pork loin, air-dried with smoked paprika and garlic. It's as lean as cured pork gets, clean, meaty and gently smoky.
cards.why: The whole loin, the long lean muscle along the back, is trimmed, rubbed with salt, pimentón and garlic, cased and dried for two months or more. With almost no fat it slices rosy and eats firm and meaty. From ibérico pigs it shows fine marbling and a nutty depth.
cards.note: Air-dried, not cooked, and served as is in thin slices.
cards.origin: Spain; lomo is Spanish for loin
cards.notThis: Not tenderloin. Lomo is the loin, the big muscle along the back. On a Latin American menu it can mean fresh beef.
cards.line: Lomo ibérico, marcona almonds, olive oil

cards.gist: Italian pork belly cured with salt and spice, air-dried, not smoked
cards.guest: It's Italian bacon without the smoke, pork belly cured with salt, pepper and spices. It tastes cleaner and sweeter than American bacon, all pork and spice.
cards.why: Same cut as bacon, the belly, but salt-cured with pepper, garlic and spices such as juniper or nutmeg, then air-dried for weeks instead of smoked. It comes as a flat slab for dicing or a rolled spiral for slicing. Without smoke, the sweet pork and spice come through.
cards.note: Usually diced and cooked crisp. Thin-sliced rolled pancetta may be served uncooked, so ask the kitchen.
cards.notThis: Not bacon, which is smoked, and not guanciale, which is the jowl. Pancetta is unsmoked belly.
cards.line: Brussels sprouts, crisp pancetta, aged balsamic

cards.gist: Brined beef, crusted in pepper and coriander, smoked, then steamed
cards.guest: It's beef cured like corned beef, then crusted in cracked pepper and coriander, smoked and steamed until tender. Peppery, smoky and rich.
cards.why: Brisket, or the fattier navel cut beside it, sits in brine for days, which seasons it through and keeps it rosy. Then a pepper and coriander rub, smoke, and a long steam that melts the tough tissue. Think corned beef with a crust and a smoky edge.
cards.note: Fully cooked. The pink color comes from the cure, not from doneness, so there is no temperature to ask for.
cards.notThis: Not corned beef, which shares the brine but is simmered, with no pepper crust and no smoke.
cards.line: House pastrami, rye, whole grain mustard, pickles

cards.gist: Ground meat, fat, often liver, baked, chilled, spread on toast
cards.guest: It's a French meat spread, usually pork and liver, baked and chilled. It can be silky or coarse, and it's rich, so a little on toast goes a long way.
cards.why: Meat, fat and usually some liver are ground with salt, spice and often brandy, packed into a mold and baked gently in a water bath. Chilled, it sets firm enough to slice. Liver gives the deep mineral richness, and fat makes it spread.
cards.note: Served cold. Liver versions are often left pink inside, so ask the kitchen how theirs is cooked.
cards.notThis: Not rillettes, which are shredded, and not foie gras, fattened duck or goose liver. A terrine is the same family, named for its mold.
cards.line: Country pâté, cornichons, Dijon, grilled sourdough

cards.gist: Italian pork leg, salted, air-dried a year or more, shaved thin
cards.guest: It's Italian ham, salted and air-dried for a year or more, never cooked or smoked. Sliced paper-thin, it's silky, a little sweet, and melts on your tongue.
cards.why: A whole hind leg is rubbed with sea salt, then hung in moving air for a year or longer. It slowly loses water while the meat's own enzymes build sweet, nutty flavor. Cut thin, the fat melts on contact. It is sweeter and softer than Spanish ham.
cards.note: Served raw, as cured. Heat turns it salty and tough, so it goes on hot dishes last.
cards.pairs: Melon, figs, burrata, arugula, breadsticks
cards.notThis: Not speck, the same leg lightly smoked, not pancetta, cured belly for cooking, and not jamón ibérico, Spain's longer-aged ham.
cards.line: Prosciutto di Parma, compressed melon, basil

cards.gist: Meat cooked slowly in its own fat, then shredded into a rich spread
cards.guest: Think pulled pork, but French and spreadable. The meat cooks for hours in its own fat until it falls apart, then it's packed in a jar and served with toast.
cards.why: Pork, duck or rabbit is salted and simmered very gently in fat until it collapses, then shredded, stirred with some of that fat and sealed in a jar under a fat cap. It is soft and stringy, not smooth, and it tastes milder than liver-rich pâté.
cards.note: Served cool, not fridge-cold, so the fat softens and spreads. The pale layer of fat on top is normal.
cards.notThis: Not pâté, which is ground and baked, usually with liver. Not confit, which is served whole, not shredded.
cards.line: Pork rillettes, grilled bread, cornichons, mustard

cards.gist: Boned pork leg cured with juniper, lightly cold smoked, then aged
cards.guest: It's a smoked cousin of prosciutto from the Italian Alps, cured with juniper and mountain herbs. It's a bit firmer, with a gentle smoky finish.
cards.why: Alto Adige sits on the Austrian border, and its ham borrows from both sides: dry cured like prosciutto, then cold smoked over beechwood. The leg is rubbed with salt, juniper, bay and pepper and aged about five months. Boned, flat and smoked, it eats firmer than prosciutto.
cards.note: Served raw, as cured. Cold smoke flavors it but does not cook it.
cards.pairs: Rye bread, pickles, horseradish, apples, mountain cheeses
cards.notThis: Not prosciutto, which is never smoked. In German the word just means bacon, so on an Austrian menu it may be bacon.
cards.line: Speck, shaved apple, horseradish cream, rye crisps

cards.gist: Cajun pork shoulder, cured, crusted in cayenne and garlic, smoked
cards.guest: It's Cajun smoked pork, rubbed with cayenne and garlic. Spicy, salty and very smoky, so the kitchen dices it small to season a dish, the way you'd use bacon.
cards.why: Called a ham, but it is not leg meat. Pork shoulder is cut into slabs, briefly cured, packed in a cayenne, garlic and paprika rub and hot smoked until cooked through. Too intense to eat by the slice, it goes into gumbo, jambalaya, beans, grits and cream sauces.
cards.origin: South Louisiana, the name likely from Spanish tasajo, dried meat
cards.notThis: Not andouille, its smokehouse partner, which is a sausage in a casing. This is a solid piece of shoulder.
cards.line: Shrimp and grits, tasso ham gravy, scallions

cards.gist: French craft of salting, smoking and preserving meat, mostly pork
cards.guest: It's the French word for cured and prepared meats, like ham, salami and pâté. A board is a selection made for sharing, with pickles, mustard and bread.
cards.why: The word comes from the French for cooked flesh and named the pork butcher's shop. Before refrigeration, salting, drying, smoking and cooking in fat were how meat lasted the winter. A good board contrasts textures: a silky ham, a firm salami, something spreadable.
cards.note: Dry-cured ham, salami and bresaola are served raw, as cured.
cards.notThis: Not a cheese board. Italy calls the same craft salumi, and salami is only one kind of it.
cards.line: Charcuterie board, house pickles, mustard, grilled bread

cards.gist: Lean beef round, salted with wine and spice, air-dried deep red
cards.guest: It's very lean air-dried beef from the Italian Alps. Deep red, tender and a little sweet, usually dressed with olive oil and lemon.
cards.why: A single muscle from the beef round is trimmed of all fat, salted with wine, pepper, juniper and garlic, then hung to dry for a month or two in the Valtellina valley of Lombardy. With almost no fat it eats dense and clean, like a beefy prosciutto.
cards.note: Served raw, sliced very thin. Once cut it dries and darkens quickly, so it is sliced to order.
cards.notThis: Not carpaccio, which is fresh raw beef. This is cured and dried for weeks, so it is firmer and saltier.
cards.line: Bresaola, arugula, lemon, shaved Parmesan

cards.gist: Coarse-cut pressed dry salami of southern Italy, often hot with chili
cards.guest: It's a rustic dry salami from southern Italy, chopped coarse so you get real pieces of pork in every slice. Meatier and bolder than everyday salami.
cards.why: Lean pork and firm fat are chopped, not finely ground, seasoned with salt, pepper and often Calabrian chili, and cased. Pressed under weights for the first days, then hung to dry for weeks, it eats dense, chewy and tangy, like a rougher Genoa salami.
cards.note: Dry-cured, never cooked. Sold hot or sweet: sweet means mild, not sugary. Know which is on the board.
cards.origin: Calabria and Basilicata, Italy; from soppressare, to press down
cards.line: Hot soppressata, aged provolone, marinated olives

cards.gist: Soft, fiery Calabrian pork salami that spreads like butter
cards.guest: It's a spicy, spreadable salami from Calabria in southern Italy. Think of a soft, smoky chili and pork spread that melts into warm bread.
cards.why: Fatty pork is ground very fine with a huge share of Calabrian chili, as much as a third by weight, then stuffed in a casing, lightly smoked and fermented. So much fat and chili keeps it from ever firming up, so it stays a brick-red paste: rich, tangy, smoky and hot.
cards.note: Cured and fermented, never cooked. Often served as it is, spread on bread.
cards.origin: Spilinga, Calabria; the name likely comes from the French andouille
cards.pairs: Grilled bread, pizza, pasta sauces, eggs, burrata, honey
cards.line: Grilled sourdough, 'nduja, burrata, honey

cards.gist: Long-aged dry ham from Spain's native black pigs, carved paper-thin
cards.guest: It's Spain's great cured ham, from black Iberian pigs and aged for years. It's nutty and a little sweet, and the fat melts on your tongue.
cards.why: The Iberian pig stores fat inside the muscle, and the top grade, bellota, fattens on acorns in oak pasture. Legs are salted, then hung 2 to 4 years. That fat is soft enough to melt at room temperature, so slices turn glossy, nutty and deeper than prosciutto.
cards.note: Served uncooked, at room temperature. White specks are crystals from long aging, not a flaw.
cards.notThis: Not prosciutto, which is Italian, from white pigs, and milder. Spain's everyday serrano also comes from white pigs.
cards.line: Hand-carved jamón ibérico de bellota, pan con tomate

cards.gist: Pork belly cured with salt and sugar, smoked, then sliced to crisp
cards.guest: It's pork belly cured with salt and a little sugar, then smoked over wood. Cooked until the fat crisps, it's salty, smoky and a touch sweet.
cards.why: Belly is layered fat and lean. About a week in salt, sugar and curing salt firms it and keeps the lean rosy, then hickory or applewood smoke adds the signature flavor. In the pan the fat renders out and the strips crisp. Lardons are short batons cut from the slab.
cards.note: Bacon labeled uncured is still cured, with celery powder standing in for curing salt.
cards.notThis: Not pancetta, the same belly cured but usually not smoked. Pork belly on a menu is the fresh cut, not cured.
cards.line: Thick-cut applewood bacon, maple, black pepper

cards.gist: Loaf of seasoned chopped meats baked in a mold, chilled and sliced
cards.guest: It's a French country-style meat loaf, served cold in slices. Think of a coarse, rich pâté you eat with a fork, with mustard and pickles.
cards.why: Seasoned chopped pork, liver and fat, often with brandy, are packed into a deep rectangular mold, also called a terrine, and baked gently in a water bath. Pressed and chilled overnight, it slices clean, showing a mosaic of meat, fat and garnish.
cards.note: Not every terrine is pork. Vegetables, fish or foie gras are layered the same way.
cards.notThis: Not quite pâté, which names the mixture and is often smooth and spreadable. A terrine is named for its mold and served sliced.
cards.line: Country pork terrine, cornichons, grain mustard, toast

cards.gist: Brisket cured in spiced salt brine, then simmered until fork-tender
cards.guest: It's beef brisket cured for days in a salty, spiced brine, then simmered until it's tender. It's pink, salty and gently spiced, the heart of a Reuben.
cards.why: Brisket sits 5 to 10 days in a brine of salt, sugar, curing salt and pickling spices such as bay, mustard seed and coriander. The cure keeps it pink, and long simmering softens the tough cut. Corn is an old word for coarse grains of salt.
cards.note: Pink here comes from the curing salt and does not mean undercooked.
cards.notThis: Not pastrami, which starts with the same kind of cure but is then rubbed in pepper and coriander and smoked.
cards.line: House corned beef Reuben, sauerkraut, Swiss, rye

cards.gist: Heavily marbled crescent of beef that wraps the outside of a rib steak
cards.guest: It's the outer strip of a ribeye, the part most people save for the last bite. You get ribeye richness with the softness of a filet.
cards.why: A ribeye is the round eye plus a thin crescent curving over it. That crescent, the spinalis, has the most marbling on the steak and a loose, open grain, so it eats softer and richer than the eye. One animal yields very little, hence the price.
cards.note: Thin, so it cooks fast. The marbling needs heat to melt, and most kitchens send it medium rare.
cards.notThis: Not coulotte, the leaner sirloin cap from the back end. Calotte and coulotte sound alike on a menu.
cards.line: Grilled ribeye cap, charred onion, bordelaise

cards.gist: Hard-working chewing muscle of the face, braised until spoon-soft
cards.guest: It's the cheek muscle, braised for hours until it cuts with a spoon. Think of the richest pot roast you've had, silkier and deeper in flavor.
cards.why: An animal chews all day, so this muscle is dense with connective tissue and tough as leather cooked fast. Braised low for three hours or more, that tissue melts into gelatin, making the meat sticky and silky and the braising liquid a glossy sauce.
cards.note: Always slow cooked through, so there is no temperature to ask the guest for.
cards.pairs: Red wine braise, polenta, mashed potato, root vegetables
cards.line: Braised beef cheek, soft polenta, red wine jus

cards.gist: One thick cut of beef from the diaphragm, loose-grained and deeply mineral
cards.guest: It's the butcher's steak, the one they used to keep for themselves. Loose grain, deep beef flavor, and usually served sliced.
cards.why: It hangs between the last rib and the loin, the thick central pillar of the diaphragm, one per animal. Bearing no weight, it stays fairly soft, but a coarse grain and rich blood supply give it a mineral flavor bolder than strip or filet. It is sliced across the grain.
cards.note: Best at medium rare. Past medium it tightens and turns chewy, so steer well-done guests elsewhere.
cards.notThis: Not skirt steak, the long thin belt of diaphragm beside it. Hanger is one short, thick piece.
cards.line: Grilled hanger steak, chimichurri, fries

cards.gist: Bony lower leg joint of a pig, usually smoked and simmered to flavor a pot
cards.guest: It's the smoked lower joint of the pork leg. It simmers in the pot for hours and gives the whole dish a deep, smoky pork flavor.
cards.why: The hock is where the leg meets the foot: mostly skin, tendon and bone with a little meat, usually cured and smoked like ham. Simmered for hours, the skin and tendon melt into gelatin that gives body to beans, greens and soups, and the smoke and salt season the pot.
cards.note: A hock often seasons a dish without showing on the plate. Mention the pork when a guest asks what is in it.
cards.pairs: Collard greens, split pea soup, white beans, black-eyed peas
cards.line: White beans, smoked ham hock, cornbread

cards.gist: Upper rib beef steak, the most marbled of the classic steakhouse cuts
cards.guest: It's the richest of the classic steaks, cut from the rib and marbled all the way through. For big beef flavor and a juicy bite, this is the one.
cards.why: It comes from high on the back over the ribs, a muscle that does little work, so it is soft and threaded with fat that melts and bastes the meat from inside. It is fattier and bolder than a strip and far richer than a filet. Roasted whole, the same cut is prime rib.
cards.note: Medium rare to medium suits it better than rare, where the fat can stay waxy.
cards.pairs: Creamed spinach, baked potato, red wine sauce, Cabernet
cards.line: 16 oz bone-in ribeye, roasted garlic butter

cards.gist: Hard-working cut above the front leg that shreds after hours of low heat
cards.guest: Shoulder is the cut made for slow cooking. After hours of low heat it pulls apart with a fork and has more flavor than any of the lean cuts.
cards.why: The front legs carry most of an animal's weight, so the shoulder is dense with connective tissue and seamed with fat, and chewy if cooked fast. Braised, smoked or slow roasted for hours, that tissue melts and the meat shreds. It is pulled pork and carnitas on a pig, pot roast on a steer.
cards.notThis: Pork butt, or Boston butt, is the upper shoulder, not the rear of the pig. The rear leg is the ham.
cards.line: Slow-roasted lamb shoulder, white beans, salsa verde

cards.gist: Fatty beef on stubby bones from low on the chest, braised until it yields
cards.guest: Short rib is thick, well-marbled beef braised for hours until it falls off the bone. Rich and soft, like pot roast turned all the way up.
cards.why: It comes from the lower rib cage, in the chuck and plate, where the meat is heavily marbled and layered with connective tissue. A long braise melts both, so the beef holds its shape but gives to a fork. Sawn thin across the bones, the same cut is grilled fast for Korean barbecue.
cards.note: Braised short rib is cooked through. There is no temperature to ask the guest for.
cards.pairs: Red wine sauce, mashed potato, polenta, horseradish
cards.line: Red wine braised short rib, potato puree, glazed carrots

cards.gist: Small tapered muscle under the spine, the softest, mildest steak cut
cards.guest: Tenderloin is the most tender cut on the animal, the one filet mignon comes from. Lean, mild and so soft you barely need the knife.
cards.why: A long, narrow muscle under the backbone that does almost no work, it has very little connective tissue and cuts like butter. The trade is flavor: lean, with little marbling, it tastes milder than a ribeye or strip, so it often comes with a sauce, a butter or a bacon wrap.
cards.note: Beef filet dries out past medium, so most kitchens suggest rare to medium rare. Pork tenderloin is always cooked further.
cards.pairs: Bearnaise, peppercorn sauce, red wine sauce, mushrooms
cards.line: 8 oz beef tenderloin, bearnaise, pommes puree

cards.gist: Fresh, uncured slab from the underside of the pig, layered fat and lean
cards.guest: It's the same cut as bacon, only fresh. It's very rich, cooked slowly until spoon tender, then crisped on the outside.
cards.why: The boneless underside of the pig, in alternating layers of fat and lean. Slow cooking melts the fat and softens the meat, then high heat crisps the surface or the skin. Rich like short rib but softer and sweeter, so portions are small and come with something sharp.
cards.pairs: Pickles, apples, mustard, bitter greens, soy and ginger glazes
cards.notThis: Not bacon, which is this cut cured and smoked, nor pancetta, cured and not smoked. Belly on a menu is fresh meat.
cards.line: Crispy pork belly, apple mostarda, mustard greens

cards.gist: Short loin steak with a firm, tight bite and a band of fat down one edge
cards.guest: It's the classic steakhouse steak, with a firmer bite and beefier flavor than filet. It's a little leaner than a ribeye, with an edge of fat that crisps on the grill.
cards.why: Cut from the short loin, along the back just behind the ribs. It is the same long back muscle as the ribeye, only further back, where it carries less marbling. That muscle does little work, so it stays tender, with a tight grain and a clean chew.
cards.origin: Named for New York steakhouses, where it became the house cut
cards.pairs: Peppercorn sauce, compound butter, creamed spinach, fries
cards.line: 14 oz New York strip, bone marrow butter, watercress

cards.gist: One large steak holding two: strip on one side, tenderloin on the other
cards.guest: It's two steaks on one T-shaped bone, a New York strip on one side and filet on the other. The porterhouse is the bigger cut, with more filet.
cards.why: Both are sawn across the short loin, so each slice catches the strip above the bone and the tenderloin below it. The tenderloin tapers toward the front, so rear steaks, with a wide filet, are porterhouses and forward ones are T-bones. USDA sets the line at 1.25 inches of filet.
cards.note: The filet side cooks faster than the strip side, so the two halves rarely land at the same doneness.
cards.pairs: Creamed spinach, hash browns, a big red wine
cards.line: Porterhouse for two, 32 oz, roasted garlic, sea salt

cards.guest: A lean, flat steak with big beefy flavor, cooked hot and fast and sliced thin across the grain, so it's tender with a little chew.
cards.why: One flat abdominal muscle from just ahead of the back legs. It works constantly, so it is lean and full of flavor, with long fibers running its whole length. Sliced thin across them it is tender, along them stringy.
cards.note: Best at medium rare to medium. With so little fat it dries out and toughens past that.

cards.gist: Long, thin ribbon of beef from under the ribs, loose grained, well marbled
cards.guest: A long, thin steak with a loose grain and rich marbling, so it's intensely beefy. It's the classic for carne asada.
cards.why: The outside skirt is the diaphragm and the inside skirt lies beside it, both from the plate. A thin belt with coarse fibers running across its width and more fat than flank, it soaks up marinade and chars fast. It wants fierce heat, then slicing across the grain.
cards.note: Best at medium rare to medium. It is so thin that it toughens quickly past that.
cards.origin: Fajitas take their name from it: faja is Spanish for belt

cards.gist: Loose, open-grained bottom sirloin steak, a French bistro favorite
cards.guest: A French bistro steak from the sirloin, next to the flank. Loose, juicy grain and deep beefy flavor, like skirt but thicker and more tender.
cards.why: It is the sirloin flap, a thin muscle where the bottom sirloin meets the flank. Its coarse, open fibers have good marbling between them, so it holds marinade and sauce, takes a hard sear and stays juicy.
cards.note: Best at medium rare, sliced across the grain. Past medium it turns chewy.
cards.origin: French for bib, bistro shorthand for flat belly-side steaks
cards.notThis: Not flank or skirt, though in France the word covers several flat cuts. Here it is sirloin flap, looser and more marbled than flank.
cards.line: Bavette steak, shallot butter, frites

cards.gist: Chuck steak with its tough center gristle cut out, nearly as tender as filet
cards.guest: Flat iron is a shoulder steak, second only to filet for tenderness. It has more marbling than filet, so it tastes beefier.
cards.why: It is the top blade muscle from the shoulder, or chuck. A thick seam of gristle runs through its middle, which kept it off menus until meat scientists in Nebraska and Florida showed, around 2002, how to cut it out, leaving two flat, well-marbled steaks.
cards.origin: Named for its shape, like an old flat clothes iron

cards.gist: Tough chest muscle of beef that turns tender only after hours of slow heat
cards.guest: Beef from the chest, cooked slowly for hours until tender and juicy, with deep beefy flavor and a rich, melting edge of fat.
cards.why: The chest muscles carry much of the steer's weight, so they are dense with connective tissue. Hours of low heat, in smoke or a braise, melt it into gelatin for a moist, silky slice. The flat is the lean half and the point the fatty half. Cured, it becomes corned beef and, often, pastrami.

cards.gist: Rounds of beef tail, braised until the meat slips off the bone
cards.guest: Oxtail is the tail of the steer, cut into thick rounds and braised for hours until it falls off the bone. It's rich, sticky and deeply beefy.
cards.why: The tail is mostly bone, cartilage and small pockets of hard-working muscle, so it is loaded with collagen. Hours of slow, wet heat melt that into gelatin, giving silky meat and a glossy, sticky sauce. Think short rib, only deeper and more gelatinous.
cards.note: Usually served on the bone, so tell guests to expect small bones.
cards.origin: Once the tail of an ox, now of any beef cattle
cards.pairs: Butter beans, rice and peas, polenta, mashed potato

cards.gist: The lower leg, all sinew around a marrow bone, braised until spoon-tender
cards.guest: Shank is the lower leg of lamb or veal, braised for hours until it's spoon-tender and slides off the bone. The sauce is made from its own rich juices.
cards.why: The lower leg carries the animal all day, so the meat is lean, tough and laced with sinew. Hours of gentle braising melt that sinew into gelatin, giving moist shreds and a sticky sauce. Lamb comes whole on the bone. Veal is often cross-cut around its marrow bone.
cards.note: A whole lamb shank is a big portion on a long bone. The marrow in a cross-cut piece is meant to be eaten.
cards.origin: Sold as lamb, veal, beef or pork; cross-cut veal shank is Italy's osso buco
cards.pairs: Polenta, saffron risotto, white beans, mashed potato
cards.line: Braised lamb shank, creamy polenta, rosemary jus

cards.gist: The triangular cap of the top sirloin, grilled under its own fat
cards.guest: Coulotte is the cap of the top sirloin, a juicy, beefy steak cooked under its own fat so it bastes itself. In Brazil it's picanha, the star of the steakhouse.
cards.why: One triangular muscle on top of the sirloin, under a thick layer of fat. It does moderate work, so it is tender enough to grill or roast but beefier than the loin steaks. Sliced across the grain it eats like a leaner, firmer strip.
cards.note: Best at medium rare to medium, with the fat cap left on.

cards.line: Grilled coulotte steak, chimichurri, charred onion

cards.gist: The rib section of a young sheep, roasted whole and carved into chops
cards.guest: Rack of lamb is the rib section, roasted whole and carved into chops on the bone. It's the most tender, mild cut of lamb, the ribeye of the animal.
cards.why: Seven or eight ribs with the eye of loin meat attached, a muscle along the back that barely works, so it is fine-grained and tender. The bones are often frenched, meaning scraped clean for looks. It is roasted fast and hot, then cut into single or double chops.
cards.note: Best at medium rare, rosy through the middle. Past medium the small eye of meat dries out quickly.
cards.pairs: Mustard and herb crust, mint, rosemary, garlic
cards.line: Herb-crusted rack of lamb, mint salsa verde, potato gratin

cards.gist: A thick slice across the hog's loin, usually on the bone, seared or grilled
cards.guest: A pork chop is a thick cut from the loin, the pig's answer to a bone-in strip or ribeye. Done right, it's seared outside and juicy in the middle.
cards.why: Chops are sliced across the loin, the long muscle down the pig's back. It does little work, so it is tender, but it is lean and dries out fast. Kitchens fight that with thick cuts, the bone left in, a brine and a rest. Rib chops carry more fat than center-cut loin chops.
cards.note: Many kitchens now cook it to a blush of pink, 63 C (145 F) plus a rest, so ask the chef how ours is cooked.
cards.pairs: Apples, mustard, sage, cabbage, cider sauce
cards.line: Brined bone-in pork chop, roasted apples, mustard jus

cards.gist: Beef from Japanese cattle breeds prized for dense, fine marbling
cards.guest: Wagyu is beef from Japanese cattle breeds famous for marbling. The fat runs all through the meat, so it's buttery, tender and so rich that a little goes a long way.
cards.why: These breeds are genetically inclined to store fat inside the muscle, not just around it, and are fed far longer than other cattle. That fat melts at a lower temperature than other beef fat, so it goes buttery in the mouth. Japan's top grade is A5. American versions are usually crossed with Angus.
cards.note: Japanese A5 is usually sold by the ounce, seared quickly and served in small portions.

cards.gist: Cold-water cousin of salmon and trout with pink, moderately rich flesh
cards.guest: It's a cold-water fish from the salmon family, and it eats right between salmon and trout. Rich but mild, with a fine flake and a thin skin that crisps.
cards.why: A member of the salmon family from icy northern lakes and coasts, now mostly farmed in cold tanks. Its fat sits between trout and salmon, so the pink to red flesh stays moist and fine-flaked, with a cleaner, milder flavor than salmon.
cards.note: Nearly all of it is farmed, mostly in Iceland and Canada. The thin skin crisps well and is meant to be eaten.
cards.notThis: Not salmon or trout, though kin to both. It is milder and finer than salmon, and richer than trout.
cards.line: Crispy-skin arctic char, fennel, citrus beurre blanc

cards.gist: Finger-long freshwater crustacean, a tiny lobster eaten for its tail
cards.guest: They're freshwater shellfish that look like tiny lobsters, a Louisiana staple. The tail meat is sweet and tender, somewhere between shrimp and lobster.
cards.why: A freshwater crustacean from Louisiana's swamps and rice ponds, built like a lobster about a finger long. Only the tail holds real meat, sweet and tender, while the fat in the head carries the flavor, so whole ones are boiled in spice and peeled by hand.
cards.note: Live season runs roughly late winter to early summer. Outside it, most kitchens cook with frozen peeled tail meat.
cards.pairs: Boils with corn, potato and sausage; étouffée over rice
cards.line: Crawfish étouffée, Carolina Gold rice, scallion

cards.gist: Wing of a ray, its sweet white flesh pulling apart in long strands
cards.guest: It's the wing of a ray, a cousin of the stingray. The meat is sweet and mild, a little like scallop or crab, and it pulls away in long tender strands.
cards.why: Skates are rays, with a skeleton of cartilage instead of bone. Only the wings are eaten: a fan of long muscle strands over a sheet of soft cartilage, so the flesh comes away in ribbons, not flakes. It is lean, sweet and mild, and takes well to a hot pan.
cards.note: No pin bones. A bone-in wing has a flat sheet of soft cartilage in the middle, and the meat slides off it with a fork.
cards.pairs: Black butter, capers, parsley and vinegar, the French classic, or brown butter and lemon
cards.line: Pan-roasted skate wing, brown butter, capers, lemon

cards.gist: Small, thin flatfish with lean, delicate, mild and sweet fillets
cards.guest: It's a small flatfish, lean and very delicate, with a mild, sweet flavor. If you like sole, it eats the same way, light and fine-flaked.
cards.why: A flatfish that lies on the seabed with both eyes on its upper side, left or right depending on the species. Little fat and thin fillets give a fine, soft texture and a mild, sweet taste. Fluke is summer flounder, and many American soles are flounders too. It cooks in minutes.
cards.note: Fluke is often served raw, sliced thin as crudo or sashimi.
cards.notThis: Not halibut, its giant cousin. Halibut comes as thick, firm portions, and flounder as thin, soft fillets or a whole fish.

cards.gist: Warm-water reef fish with lean, firm white meat in big chunky flakes
cards.guest: It's a mild white fish from the Gulf and the South Atlantic. The meat is firm and sweet with big, moist flakes, so it holds up to the grill or the fryer.
cards.why: A heavy-bodied reef fish of the sea bass family, caught off Florida, the Gulf and the Carolinas. It is lean but holds moisture well, and thick fillets break into large, firm flakes. The flavor is mild and faintly sweet, close to sea bass.
cards.notThis: Not snapper, the other Southern reef fish. Snapper fillets are thinner and finer-flaked, and grouper is chunkier and firmer.

cards.gist: The largest flatfish, cut into thick, firm, snow-white lean portions
cards.guest: It's a big cold-water flatfish with thick, snow-white meat. Firm, clean and mildly sweet, the fish for someone who wants nothing fishy.
cards.why: The giant of the flatfish, a right-eyed flounder that can outweigh a person, from the cold North Pacific and North Atlantic. Its size gives thick portions with a firm, large flake. With very little fat, it tastes clean and mild and leans on sauce for richness.
cards.note: So lean it dries out fast. Kitchens pull it just as it turns opaque, and it is a poor choice for well done.
cards.origin: Middle English haly butte, holy flatfish, eaten on feast days
cards.notThis: Not flounder, a small flatfish sold in thin fillets, or turbot, which is richer and more gelatinous.
