cards.gist: Blue-black bivalve with soft, sweet meat, steamed open in its own broth
cards.guest: They're shellfish in blue-black shells, steamed until they pop open. The meat is soft and sweet, milder than a clam, and the broth is made for dipping bread.
cards.why: A bivalve farmed in clusters on ropes, which keeps sand out. Steamed a few minutes with wine, garlic and shallot, the shells open and release their own liquor, which becomes the broth. The meat is plump and soft, sweeter and less briny than clam or oyster.
cards.note: A mussel still shut after steaming should be left in the bowl, not pried open. Orange or cream meat is only male or female.
cards.notThis: Not clams. Mussels have thin, blue-black teardrop shells and soft meat. Clams are rounder, paler and chewier.
cards.line: Steamed mussels, white wine, garlic, grilled bread

cards.gist: Rough-shelled bivalve, often eaten raw, that tastes of its home water
cards.guest: They're shellfish, and on the half shell they're shucked to order and eaten raw. A cold, silky bite of clean ocean, some brinier, some sweeter.
cards.why: A bivalve that filters the water it grows in, so each bay gives its own flavor, the way a vineyard does for wine. East Coast ones run briny and firm, West Coast ones sweeter and creamier, with a cucumber or melon note.
cards.note: On the half shell they come raw and alive on ice, opened to order. The list changes daily, so learn each name and where it grew.

cards.gist: Eggs of a female fish, cured loose or cooked whole in the sac
cards.guest: Roe is fish eggs. Salmon roe pops with a bright, salty burst, and spring shad roe is seared whole until it is creamy inside.
cards.why: Roe is the egg mass of a female fish, held in a thin sac. Loosened and salted, the eggs pop and taste of the sea: salmon roe is large and orange, flying fish roe tiny and crunchy. Cooked whole in the sac, like shad roe, it firms outside and turns creamy and grainy within.
cards.note: Loose salted roe, like salmon roe, is cured but never cooked: it is served raw.
cards.pairs: Blini, sour cream, chives, sushi rice, brown butter, bacon
cards.notThis: Caviar on its own means salted sturgeon roe. Any other roe sold as caviar has to name the fish, as in salmon caviar.
cards.line: Salmon roe, buckwheat blini, sour cream, chives

cards.gist: Rich, oily pink fish that grows at sea and spawns back in rivers
cards.guest: Salmon is rich and buttery, with big, silky flakes. Wild king is the richest of all, and sockeye is leaner and deeper in flavor.
cards.why: Salmon hatch in rivers, fatten at sea and swim back upstream to spawn, so they carry fat for the trip. It keeps the flesh moist and gives it big, soft flakes. The color comes from a pigment in the krill and shrimp they eat. King is the fattiest species, sockeye the reddest.
cards.note: Often served medium, still translucent in the center. Guests can ask for it cooked through.
cards.origin: Wild from Alaska to California; Atlantic salmon on menus is almost always farmed
cards.notThis: Arctic char and trout look alike but are milder, with a finer flake. Steelhead is a sea-run trout that eats much like salmon.

cards.gist: Sweet round muscle a shellfish uses to clap its two shells shut
cards.guest: Scallops are the sweet muscle that snaps the shell shut, seared golden on the outside and soft, almost creamy, in the middle.
cards.why: A scallop swims by clapping its shells, driven by one big muscle, and that muscle is what we eat. It is rich in glycogen and sweet amino acids, so it tastes sweet and browns well. Sea scallops are large and sear. Bay scallops are small and cook in seconds. Untreated dry ones sear best.
cards.note: Best seared golden and left just translucent in the center. Cooked through, they turn rubbery.
cards.notThis: Not king trumpet mushroom scallops, which are thick rounds of mushroom stem cut to look like the real thing.
cards.line: Seared sea scallops, cauliflower puree, brown butter

cards.gist: Red-skinned warm-reef fish, lean and sweet, often served whole
cards.guest: Snapper is a mild, slightly sweet white fish from warm Gulf waters. It is lean and flaky, and the skin crisps up beautifully.
cards.why: Snapper live on warm reefs in the Gulf of Mexico and the southern Atlantic. They are lean, so the flesh is mild and sweet with moist, medium flakes, and the red skin crisps well in a hot pan. Whole snapper, fried or grilled, is a classic of the Gulf and the Caribbean.
cards.note: Served whole, it arrives on the bone, with fins and small bones to work around.
cards.notThis: Not grouper, which is firmer and chunkier. West Coast Pacific snapper is usually rockfish, a different fish.
cards.line: Whole fried red snapper, green mango slaw, lime

cards.gist: Ancient armored river fish, dense and meaty, prized for its eggs
cards.guest: Sturgeon is the fish caviar comes from. The meat is firm and rich, more like veal than a flaky fish, and it is wonderful smoked.
cards.why: Sturgeon have barely changed in 200 million years: rows of bony plates, not ordinary scales, and a skeleton mostly of cartilage. The flesh has almost no flake and a good amount of fat, so it eats dense and meaty, often compared to veal or lobster, and it takes smoke beautifully.
cards.origin: Mostly farmed white sturgeon from California and Idaho; wild stocks are protected
cards.pairs: Potato pancakes, sour cream, dill, horseradish, rye bread
cards.line: Smoked sturgeon, potato pancake, sour cream, dill

cards.gist: Lean deep-water fish that eats crab, sweet and firm like lobster
cards.guest: Tilefish is a lean white fish from deep Atlantic waters. It eats crab and shrimp, so it tastes sweet, a little like lobster, with firm, moist flakes.
cards.why: Golden tilefish live at the edge of the continental shelf, digging burrows in the clay and feeding on crabs and shrimp. That diet is why the flesh tastes so sweet, often compared to lobster or scallop. It is lean, with a firm, fine flake closer to halibut than to cod.
cards.origin: Deep Atlantic shelf edge, from New England down to the Gulf of Mexico

cards.gist: Mild, delicate freshwater fish, often pan-fried whole or split
cards.guest: Trout is a mild, delicate freshwater fish with tender flakes and thin skin that crisps in the pan. With brown butter and almonds, it is a classic.
cards.why: Most trout on menus is farmed rainbow trout, raised in cold spring water in places like Idaho. It is small and fairly lean, so the flesh is mild with fine, soft flakes and the skin is thin enough to eat crisp. Steelhead is rainbow trout that went to sea: bigger, richer and pinker.
cards.note: Served whole, it keeps its fine rib bones, and butterflied fillets can still hold a few small pin bones.
cards.notThis: Arctic char is a cousin with richer, pinker flesh. Salmon is bigger and much oilier.

cards.gist: Prized European flatfish, firm and white, rich in gelatin at the bone
cards.guest: Turbot is one of the most prized fish in Europe, a flatfish with firm, snow-white flesh that is sweet and almost silky. It is often roasted whole.
cards.why: Turbot lie flat on the seabed, and their thick, muscular fillets eat firm and meaty rather than flaky. The skin and bones are rich in gelatin, which keeps the flesh moist and gives cooked turbot a silky, sticky richness that chefs pair with butter sauces.
cards.note: Often cooked on the bone to keep it juicy, so it may arrive whole or as a bone-in cut.
cards.origin: European coasts from Norway to the Mediterranean, much of it farmed in Spain
cards.notThis: Not halibut, a bigger, leaner flatfish. Cheap Greenland turbot is a different, softer and oilier fish.

cards.gist: Deep-water Carolina fish that gathers at wrecks, with big flakes
cards.guest: It's a deep-water fish from off the Carolinas, firm and mild with big white flakes. It eats a lot like grouper.
cards.why: It lives far down on rocky ledges off South Carolina and Georgia, and got its name from gathering around shipwrecks. Caught by hook and line in a small fishery, it is lean with large, moist, sweet flakes, much like grouper or a big sea bass.
cards.origin: Southeast US, the deep Charleston Bump; named for hanging around wrecks
cards.notThis: Not grouper, though it eats like one. It is its own deep-water family and a local Carolina catch.
cards.line: Pan-roasted wreckfish, Carolina Gold rice, brown butter

cards.gist: Salt-cured sturgeon eggs, served cold by the small spoonful
cards.guest: It's sturgeon roe, lightly salted and served cold. Each pearl pops with a clean, briny, buttery flavor, best with a blini and a glass of Champagne.
cards.why: Eggs are taken from a sturgeon, screened, and lightly salted, which firms them and seasons them without cooking. Nearly all caviar today is farmed, since wild sturgeon were overfished and wild Caspian caviar is barely traded. Osetra, Kaluga and Siberian are common kinds.
cards.note: Served cold and never cooked. Kitchens often use a mother-of-pearl or bone spoon rather than metal.
cards.pairs: Blini, crème fraîche, chives, potato chips, Champagne or cold vodka
cards.notThis: Not just any fish eggs. On a US menu, salmon or trout eggs must name the fish, as in salmon caviar.
cards.line: Osetra caviar, buckwheat blini, crème fraîche, chives

cards.gist: Salted, pressed and dried fish-egg sac, grated like a cheese
cards.guest: It's cured fish roe, dried into an amber block and grated over the dish. Salty and savory, it tastes like the sea's answer to parmesan.
cards.why: The whole roe sac of a grey mullet or a tuna is salted, pressed and air-dried for weeks until firm and amber. Drying concentrates it into a salty, savory, faintly bitter seasoning. Mullet is milder and more delicate, tuna darker and stronger.
cards.note: Cured and dried, never cooked. It is shaved or grated over the dish at the end.
cards.origin: Italian, from Sardinia and Sicily; the word comes from Arabic

cards.gist: Mild, lean Mediterranean white fish, often roasted and served whole
cards.guest: It's a Mediterranean sea bass, mild and delicate with crisp skin. It's often roasted whole with lemon and herbs, simple and light.
cards.why: The European sea bass, now mostly farmed in Greece and Turkey. Each fish is only a pound or two, so it suits one plate whole or as two fillets. The flesh is lean, white and finely flaked with a clean, sweet flavor, and the thin skin crisps well.
cards.note: Served whole, it comes with bones and head on. Many kitchens will fillet it before or at the table.
cards.origin: Italian name for the European sea bass; loup de mer in French
cards.notThis: Not black sea bass, the wild Atlantic fish. Branzino is the Mediterranean one, usually farmed.
cards.line: Whole roasted branzino, lemon, capers, herbs

cards.gist: Small wild Atlantic fish with firm, fine white flesh and crisp skin
cards.guest: It's a small wild fish from the Atlantic coast, sweet and delicate, and the skin crisps beautifully in the pan.
cards.why: A small grouper relative caught from New England to the Gulf by pot, hook and trawl. It stays small, a few pounds at most, so fillets are thin with a fine flake. The white flesh is sweet and mild, firmer than branzino, and the dark skin sears crisp.
cards.note: Thin fillets can hold a few fine pin bones.
cards.origin: US Atlantic coast, from Cape Cod down to Florida and the Gulf
cards.notThis: Not Chilean sea bass, a rich deep-water fish, and not branzino, the farmed Mediterranean one.
cards.line: Crispy-skin black sea bass, clams, fennel broth

cards.gist: Firm, buttery warm-water fish, often served raw, sturdy on a grill
cards.guest: Cobia is a firm, rich white fish from warm waters. It's buttery and clean served raw, and it holds up beautifully on the grill.
cards.why: A fast-swimming fish of warm seas, caught in the Gulf and farmed in open-ocean pens. It carries more fat than most white fish, so the meat is firm, moist and buttery with a clean, sweet flavor. Think somewhere between swordfish and snapper.
cards.note: Often served raw as crudo. Cooked, it stays moist even a little past medium.
cards.origin: Warm seas worldwide; Gulf anglers call it ling or lemonfish
cards.line: Cobia crudo, citrus, chili, olive oil

cards.gist: Big ocean hunter cut into thick, dense, mild steaks that grill well
cards.guest: Swordfish is meaty and mild, cut into thick steaks. It eats almost like a pork chop, great off the grill for someone who wants hearty fish.
cards.why: A large open-ocean fish, cut crosswise from the loin into boneless steaks. The flesh is dense with a tight grain and moderate fat, so it holds together on a grill and rarely breaks into flakes. It tastes mild, without the red-meat depth of tuna.
cards.note: The dark red band in each steak is the bloodline and is normal. Cooked past medium, it dries out fast.
cards.notThis: Not tuna, the other ocean steak. Swordfish is pale and cooked further, tuna deep red and served rare.
cards.line: Grilled swordfish, salsa verde, charred lemon

cards.gist: Deep-red, meaty ocean fish, served raw or seared rare inside
cards.guest: It's a meaty, deep-red fish, clean and rich. It's usually served raw, or seared outside and rare inside, closer to a steak than a flaky fish.
cards.why: Tuna are warm-bodied ocean sprinters, and their muscle is full of oxygen-carrying myoglobin, which makes it red and beefy. Yellowfin is lean, bigeye a little richer, and bluefin belly is marbled with fat. Albacore is the paler, milder one canned as white tuna.
cards.note: Usually served raw or rare. Cooked through, it firms up, dries and tastes like canned tuna.
cards.pairs: Soy, sesame, ginger, avocado, wasabi, citrus
cards.line: Seared ahi tuna, sesame, cucumber, ponzu

cards.gist: Dense, firm tail of a big-mouthed Atlantic fish, meaty and sweet
cards.guest: It's a firm, sweet white fish people call poor man's lobster. It holds together like a steak instead of flaking.
cards.why: Monkfish is an anglerfish, mostly head and mouth, so the tail is the main cut sold. That tail is dense, springy muscle around one central bone, with no flakes, so it eats sweet and meaty like shellfish and stands up to roasting, grilling and stews.
cards.note: A thin gray membrane is trimmed off first, or it shrinks and toughens in the pan.
cards.origin: North Atlantic anglerfish, sold as lotte on French menus

cards.gist: Small ten-legged crustacean, sweet and snappy, sized by count
cards.guest: Sweet, firm shrimp, cooked just until they curl and turn pink, so they stay juicy with a little snap.
cards.why: Shrimp are ten-legged crustaceans, wild or farmed, from the Gulf to Asia. The meat is almost pure muscle protein that tightens fast in heat, so a minute too long turns it rubbery. Size is a count per pound: 16/20 means 16 to 20 shrimp, U-15 means under 15.
cards.note: The dark line down the back is the digestive tract. Kitchens usually pull it out, mostly for looks and grit.

cards.gist: Chesapeake swimmer prized for sweet, hand-picked lump meat
cards.guest: It's the East Coast crab Maryland crab cakes are famous for. The meat is sweet and delicate, and the big jumbo lumps are the prize.
cards.why: A swimming crab of the Atlantic and Gulf with paddle-shaped back legs. The two big muscles driving those paddles give jumbo lump, the whitest, sweetest meat. Lump and backfin are smaller pieces, and claw meat is darker and stronger. Picking is slow handwork, hence the price.
cards.note: Hand-picked meat can hold small bits of shell and cartilage, even when picked carefully.
cards.origin: Atlantic and Gulf coasts, most famously Maryland's Chesapeake Bay
cards.pairs: Old Bay, drawn butter, crab cakes, remoulade, cold beer

cards.gist: Freshly molted Chesapeake swimmer, eaten whole with its legs
cards.guest: It's a blue crab caught just after it sheds its old shell, so you eat the whole thing. Crisp outside, sweet and juicy inside.
cards.why: Crabs grow by molting: they split the old shell and back out soft. Within hours the new one starts to firm, so watermen hold molting crabs in tanks and pull them the moment they emerge. The kitchen trims the face, gills and apron, then fries or sautés it whole.
cards.note: Eaten entirely, legs and all. The light crunch of the new shell is the point, not a mistake.
cards.origin: A late spring to summer delicacy, mostly from the Chesapeake Bay
cards.line: Fried soft-shell crab, remoulade, pickled green tomato

cards.gist: Big-clawed cold-water crustacean with a firm, sweet tail
cards.guest: It's the cold-water Atlantic kind with big claws. The tail is firm and sweet, the claw meat softer, and it all loves butter.
cards.why: A North Atlantic crustacean fished mostly off Maine and Canada. The tail is one big muscle, so it eats firm and snappy, while claws and knuckles are sweeter and softer. The meat breaks down fast after death, so it is cooked live or killed just before.
cards.note: The green paste in the body is tomalley, and dark beads in a female are roe, called coral, which turn red when cooked.
cards.notThis: Not spiny or rock lobster, a warm-water cousin with no big claws, usually sold as tails.

cards.gist: Sand-burrowing two-shelled shellfish, briny and chewy
cards.guest: Clams are briny little shellfish with a pleasant chew. Small ones like littlenecks are eaten raw or steamed open in wine and garlic.
cards.why: Two-shelled animals that burrow in sand and mud and filter the water, so they taste of where they grew. Hard shells sell by size: littlenecks small and tender, cherrystones bigger, chowder clams biggest, tough and chopped. Soft-shell steamers have a neck skin to peel.
cards.note: Sold alive with shells shut. Littlenecks and cherrystones are often served raw on the half shell.
cards.notThis: Not mussels, which are longer, blue-black and smooth, and cling to rocks and ropes instead of burrowing.
cards.line: Linguine with littleneck clams, white wine, chili
